ny_poke_o_moonshine_main_face.blurb:
The Main Face is the big gneiss cliff on Poke-O-Moonshine Mountain, in the northeastern Adirondacks beside I-87, and one of the region's best-known traditional crags. The wall is broken into named sections, and most lines run from one to several pitches.

The climbing is mostly trad on cracks, corners and slabs, concentrated from 5.9 to 5.12, with a smaller number of bolted lines and a few aid routes; in winter the cliff holds ice. It suits parties comfortable placing their own gear and managing multi-pitch descents.
ny_poke_o_moonshine_main_face.approach: The main trail starts near the old campground and follows the base of the cliff to the different sections, with the Discord section the first main landmark.

ga_zahnd_natural_area.blurb:
Zahnd is a sandstone bouldering area on Lookout Mountain in northwest Georgia, close to Cloudland Canyon and a short drive from Rocktown. It is much quieter than its neighbours; a handful of cars at the pull-off is a normal day.

Problems run from friendly V0 slabs through a deep middle at V3 to V7 and up to V10 and beyond, with a few trad lines as well. Part of the rock carries small embedded pebbles that are rougher on the skin than the better-known Georgia sandstone. It suits climbers who want solitude and a mix of grades.
ga_zahnd_natural_area.approach: A short walk of about five minutes from the pull-off leads to a small warm-up area; the other boulders are spread out beyond it.

ca_jailhouse_rock.blurb:
Jailhouse Rock is a steep sport crag on a basalt lava flow near Sonora, above the Stanislaus River between Lake Tulloch and New Melones Reservoir. The main wall is a large overhanging amphitheatre rising to about two hundred feet.

The routes are hard: from the low 5.11s into the 5.14s, with most lines at 5.13 and 5.14. The steep rock stays dry through winter storms, so it works when other Sierra foothill crags are wet. It suits strong sport climbers after sustained, overhanging lines.
ca_jailhouse_rock.approach: The trail climbs uphill from the access road to the base of the amphitheatre in around fifteen minutes.

ky_chocolate_factory.blurb:
The Chocolate Factory is one of the walls inside the Bald Rock Fork Recreational Preserve in the Red River Gorge, a property held for climbers. It is known for steep, overhanging sandstone and is mostly a sport destination, with a few trad lines and some bouldering.

Routes run from 5.7 up to 5.14, with the bulk at 5.11 and 5.12, and the angle keeps much of the wall climbable in light rain. It suits climbers after powerful, pumpy sport routes in a quieter section of the Gorge.

wa_middle_east_wall.blurb:
A north-facing palisade of basalt columns at Frenchman Coulee near Vantage, coloured with orange and yellow lichen. The lines are mostly cracks from 5.5 to 5.12 with the bulk at 5.10 and 5.11, with far fewer bolted routes than the neighbouring south-facing walls and grades a notch harder.

The wall sees few climbers, so the upper sections of routes can be dirty and anchors can be sparse. It suits experienced parties with a full rack, slings and rappel rings, and it stays cool on hot days because the sun only reaches it early and late.
wa_middle_east_wall.approach: From the main climbers' lot, follow the road to the lower trail and take the switchbacks that drop west from the central Middle East routes to the base of the wall.

nh_devil_s_den_2.blurb:
A cliff in the backcountry of Pawtuckaway State Park, reached separately from the main park entrance. It offers trad lines from 5.4 to 5.13 and a few bolted routes, with longer pitches than most of the park and a handful of multi-pitch climbs, plus boulders from V0 to V13 close by.

Crowds are lighter than at the Upper Cliff. The rock is textured and grippy; bolts vary in age and condition, so treat them with care. Autumn is the favourite season, and spring and early summer bring heavy black flies and mosquitoes.
nh_devil_s_den_2.parking_note: From exit 5 off Route 101 in Raymond, follow the road to Reservation Road, where pavement turns to dirt. Go left through the orange gate and follow the rough road a few miles to the steep hill, then park where the road allows.

tn_sunset_north.blurb:
The northern stretch of the sandstone cliff line along the west brow of Lookout Mountain above Chattanooga, widely regarded as the birthplace of the city's climbing. Traditional routes dominate, from 5.4 to the 5.13s with most at 5.10 and 5.11, and many can be led or top-roped.

The rock is high-quality sandstone and the cliff sits in shade for most of the day, so it is chilly in winter and comfortable in summer. It suits trad climbers of every level and beginners after top-rope laps.
tn_sunset_north.parking_note: Drive up Lookout Mountain to West Brow Road at the rim, where the small lot holds only a handful of cars and has a short time limit. If it is full, park lower down at the climbers' lot or near the Cravens House rather than on the street.
tn_sunset_north.approach: From the rim parking, a short walk of about five minutes leads along the brow to the base of the main overlook buttress and the cliff line to its north.

mt_gregory.blurb:
The busiest sector of the Billings Rimrocks, the sandstone cliff band wrapping the edge of town just west of the airport. More than a hundred routes mix sport, trad and top-rope lines, from easy 5.5 slabs to hard 5.13 faces, with most from 5.9 to 5.12.

The sandstone can be loose and rockfall is a real concern, so helmets and belaying well back from the base are wise. Some walls face south and bake once the sun is high, so early starts pay off in warm months.
mt_gregory.parking_note: From Rimrock Road, take Gregory Drive to Gregory Drive North and Rockwood Circle. Park along the residential streets without blocking driveways; the trail begins at the end of Rockwood Circle.
mt_gregory.approach: Follow the trail from the end of Rockwood Circle up to the base of the cliffs.
